quizName: DMV Practice Test #6 50 Questions • Passing Score 40

questions.question: Your riding clothes should protect you from all of the following, except:

options.text: Sunburn.
Windburn.
Chapped lips.
Dehydration.

questions.correctAnswerText: Chapped lips.
questions.explanation: Riding clothes should protect you from sunburn, windburn, rain, dehydration, cold, and motorcycle parts. Good clothing also helps protect you in a crash.

questions.question: A pre-ride inspection should:

options.text: Only take a few minutes.
Take more than an hour.
Be complicated to perform.
Not be done before every ride.

questions.correctAnswerText: Only take a few minutes.
questions.explanation: Check your motorcycle before every ride. A thorough inspection usually takes only a few minutes.

questions.question: When another vehicle passes you, all of the following are hazards, except:

options.text: Extended mirrors.
Objects being thrown from other vehicles.
Blasts of wind.
Headlights.

questions.correctAnswerText: Headlights.
questions.explanation: When being passed, watch out for the passing vehicle's mirrors hitting you. Also be aware of wind gusts from the passing vehicle and objects that passengers might throw.

questions.question: To swerve correctly, you should:

options.text: Shift your weight quickly.
Turn the handlebars quickly.
Press the handle grip in the direction you want to swerve.
Press the handle grip in the opposite direction of where you want to swerve.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handle grip in the direction you want to swerve.
questions.explanation: To swerve and avoid a hazard, apply slight pressure to the handle grip in your desired direction. To swerve left, press the left grip, then the right to straighten. To swerve right, press the right grip, then the left.

questions.question: Small vehicles can appear ______ and seem to be traveling ______ than they actually are.

options.text: Farther away, more slowly
Farther away, faster
Closer, more slowly
Closer, faster

questions.correctAnswerText: Farther away, more slowly
questions.explanation: Small vehicles like motorcycles often look farther away and slower than they really are. This makes it hard for other drivers to judge a motorcycle's true location and speed.

questions.question: A motorcycle operator can slow down by:

options.text: Downshifting.
Upshifting.
Cross-shifting.
Rolling on the throttle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Downshifting.
questions.explanation: Downshifting is a way to slow down a motorcycle. Remember that downshifting does not turn on the brake lights.

questions.question: A rectangular sign may be a:

options.text: School crossing sign.
Railroad crossing sign.
Stop sign.
Speed limit sign.

questions.correctAnswerText: Speed limit sign.
questions.explanation: Rectangular signs with white backgrounds and black letters show road rules like speed limits. You must follow all rules on these signs.

questions.question: If rain starts while you are riding, you should:

options.text: Ride down the center of the lane.
Increase your speed.
Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
Pull onto the shoulder of the road.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
questions.explanation: The center of a lane can be slippery when wet due to oil buildup. Ride in the tire tracks left by cars when it rains. Slow down on wet roads.

questions.question: To reduce your reaction time, you should:

options.text: Shift into neutral when slowing.
Cover the clutch and the brakes.
Pull in the clutch when turning.
Ride under the speed limit.

questions.correctAnswerText: Cover the clutch and the brakes.
questions.explanation: In high-risk areas like intersections, shopping areas, school zones, and construction zones, keep your hand near the clutch and brakes. This reduces the time you need to react to hazards.

questions.question: When approaching an uneven surface like a bump or pothole, rise slightly off your seat:

options.text: So you can jump off the motorcycle if you need to.
So your legs can absorb the shock.
So other drivers can see you better.
So you can get a better view of the uneven surface.

questions.correctAnswerText: So your legs can absorb the shock.
questions.explanation: Rising off your seat lets your joints absorb some of the impact from an uneven surface. This helps prevent the impact from throwing you off the motorcycle.

questions.question: When riding at night, which of the following should you NOT do?

options.text: Use your high beam.
Use the headlights of vehicles ahead to help you see.
Be visible.
Ride only in the left portion of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride only in the left portion of your lane.
questions.explanation: When riding at night, use your high beam (unless you are following or meeting another vehicle), use the headlights of other vehicles to help you see, and wear reflective materials to stay visible. Change your lane position as needed to see better, be seen, and have enough space around you.

questions.question: When you stop, what should you do?

options.text: Apply the rear brake first.
Apply the front brake first.
Apply both brakes at the same time.
Use only one brake, front or rear.

questions.correctAnswerText: Apply both brakes at the same time.
questions.explanation: Use both brakes every time you slow down or stop. Always apply them at the same time.

questions.question: Before carrying a passenger in traffic for the first time, what should you do?

options.text: Read books about carrying passengers.
Practice riding on an empty road.
Flash your lights so others can see you.
Practice riding on the shoulder of a road.

questions.correctAnswerText: Practice riding on an empty road.
questions.explanation: Before carrying a passenger or heavy load in traffic for the first time, practice on a quiet road. This helps you get used to how your motorcycle handles with the extra weight.

questions.question: When someone follows you too closely, what should you do?

options.text: Speed up.
Not worry about them and focus on the road ahead.
Change lanes and let them pass.
Ride on the shoulder and let them pass.

questions.correctAnswerText: Change lanes and let them pass.
questions.explanation: The best way to handle a tailgater is to change lanes and let them pass. Speeding up may make them tailgate you at a higher speed, which is more dangerous. Never ride on the shoulder because drivers do not expect you to be there and may suddenly leave the road.

questions.question: After entering a turn and rolling on the throttle, what should you do?

options.text: Always slow down.
Keep a steady speed or speed up slowly.
Speed up quickly.
Not worry about your speed.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep a steady speed or speed up slowly.
questions.explanation: Roll on the throttle through a turn to keep your suspension stable. Maintain a steady speed or speed up slowly through the turn.

questions.question: When might you need less space between you and other vehicles?

options.text: When the pavement is slippery.
When you cannot see through the vehicle ahead.
When weather and traffic conditions are perfect.
When traffic is heavy.

questions.correctAnswerText: When weather and traffic conditions are perfect.
questions.explanation: You need more space when conditions are not perfect. Increase your following distance if the pavement is slippery, you cannot see through the vehicle in front of you, or traffic is heavy.

questions.question: Why is riding directly alongside another vehicle dangerous?

options.text: You may have a hard time getting to a highway exit.
You may be in the other vehicle's blind spot.
You may block the driver's view.
It prevents other drivers from passing both of you.

questions.correctAnswerText: You may be in the other vehicle's blind spot.
questions.explanation: Riding alongside another vehicle is dangerous because you could be in their blind spot. The driver may move into your lane without seeing you. The vehicle also blocks your way to escape if a hazard appears.

questions.question: When riding, what is the correct way to look through a turn?

options.text: Turn your head and shoulders to look through turns.
Keep your arms straight.
Keep your knees away from the gas tank.
Turn only your head and eyes to look where you are going.

questions.correctAnswerText: Turn only your head and eyes to look where you are going.
questions.explanation: When turning, look through the turn by turning only your head and eyes toward where you want to go. Keep your knees against the gas tank to help you balance while turning. Keep your arms slightly bent when holding the handgrips.

questions.question: When it starts to rain, what is usually best to do?

options.text: Increase your speed.
Exit the road.
Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
Ride in the center of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
questions.explanation: The center of a lane is especially dangerous when wet. When it starts to rain, ride in the tire tracks left by cars to avoid the center of the road. The left tire track is usually the best choice.

questions.question: What is true about more than half of all motorcycle crashes?

options.text: They happen at speeds greater than 35 mph.
They are caused by worn tires.
They happen in the dark.
They involve riders with little experience on their motorcycles.

questions.correctAnswerText: They involve riders with little experience on their motorcycles.
questions.explanation: Most motorcycle crashes involve riders with little experience on their motorcycle.

questions.question: What should you do to reduce your chance of a crash?

options.text: Use your turn signals when you plan to change lanes.
Tailgate other drivers.
Look only 15 feet ahead of your motorcycle.
Do not use your headlight during the day.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use your turn signals when you plan to change lanes.
questions.explanation: To reduce crash risk, be visible to others. Signal your moves. Keep space between you and other vehicles. Look ahead at least 12 seconds. Notice dangers early. Be ready for changes.

questions.question: What should you do with mirror checks?

options.text: They are not important.
Do them only on long trips.
Make them part of your regular scanning routine.
They do not help because you cannot change what is behind you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Make them part of your regular scanning routine.
questions.explanation: Check your mirrors often as part of normal riding. Always use mirrors before changing lanes, at intersections, and before slowing down.

questions.question: A motorcycle fits you properly if:

options.text: Your feet can touch the ground when you sit on it.
You can reach the controls by stretching.
The handlebars go over your head.
Your feet cannot rest on the foot pegs.

questions.correctAnswerText: Your feet can touch the ground when you sit on it.
questions.explanation: A good fit means your feet can reach the ground when seated. You should easily reach and operate all controls.

questions.question: As the motorcycle's weight moves forward while braking, what can you do?

options.text: Apply the front brake harder.
Use less pressure on the front brake.
Apply the rear brake harder.
Lose traction.

questions.correctAnswerText: Apply the front brake harder.
questions.explanation: When you brake, your weight shifts forward. This gives the front wheel more grip. You can apply more braking force to the front brake.

questions.question: What is a danger of riding next to parked cars?

options.text: You may not find a parking spot.
A car door or driver may suddenly move into your path.
Other drivers may be looking for parking spots.
The road may be uneven.

questions.correctAnswerText: A car door or driver may suddenly move into your path.
questions.explanation: Parked cars are dangerous. Drivers may pull out without looking. Doors may open into your lane. People may step out between cars.

questions.question: What should you do when riding on a slippery surface?

options.text: Go faster.
Make sudden moves.
Move to the edge of the road.
Ride in the tire tracks left by other cars.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the tire tracks left by other cars.
questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, slow down. Avoid sudden moves. Stay away from the road edge. Ride in the tire tracks of other vehicles.

questions.question: Which sign is yellow with black lettering or symbols?

options.text: Warning
Service
Regulatory
Speed limit

questions.correctAnswerText: Warning
questions.explanation: Warning signs are yellow with black lettering or symbols. They alert you to upcoming road conditions.

questions.question: When riding downhill on a motorcycle with a sidecar, how does stopping compare to riding without a sidecar?

options.text: Stopping is easier.
Stopping takes longer.
You cannot stop.
Stopping is about the same.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stopping takes longer.
questions.explanation: A sidecar adds extra weight. Extra weight means you need more braking force. Downhill riding also increases stopping distance. Together, these make stopping longer than without a sidecar.

questions.question: How should you adjust for a passenger's added weight?

options.text: Ride slower than usual.
Keep a shorter distance between you and other vehicles.
Ride faster than usual.
Brake later than usual.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride slower than usual.
questions.explanation: A passenger adds weight. Your motorcycle needs more time to speed up, slow down, and turn. Ride slower. Slow down earlier than normal. Keep more distance from other vehicles. Find larger gaps when merging or crossing traffic.

questions.question: Where should inexperienced riders position themselves in a group?

options.text: At the front of the group.
Right behind the leader.
At the back of the group.
Wherever they are most comfortable.

questions.correctAnswerText: Right behind the leader.
questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the leader near the front. This way, experienced riders at the back can watch them and help if needed.

questions.question: When is it most important to flash your brake light?

options.text: When passing another vehicle.
When you need to slow down suddenly.
When there is a stop sign ahead.
When your signals do not work.

questions.correctAnswerText: When you need to slow down suddenly.
questions.explanation: A motorcycle has only one brake light, which is harder to notice than the two larger brake lights on cars or trucks. Flashing your brake light helps warn other drivers, especially when you need to stop faster than they expect.

questions.question: Why should you practice using convex mirrors if your motorcycle has them?

options.text: Most people are not used to using mirrors.
They make objects look farther away than they really are.
They make objects look closer than they really are.
It is difficult to remember to look at mirrors while riding.

questions.correctAnswerText: They make objects look farther away than they really are.
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors give you a wider view of the road behind you than flat mirrors do. However, they make objects appear farther away than they actually are. You should get used to how your mirrors work before riding.

questions.question: If hazards are on your left, where should you ride in your lane?

options.text: In the left portion of the lane.
In the right portion of the lane.
In any portion of the lane.
On the shoulder.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the right portion of the lane.
questions.explanation: When hazards are on your left, ride in the right portion of the lane to avoid them. Always be ready to change your position as conditions on the road and traffic change.

questions.question: What vest or jacket color helps you be seen the best?

options.text: Red
Black
Silver
Blue

questions.correctAnswerText: Red
questions.explanation: Wear bright clothing while riding to be more visible to other drivers. Bright red, orange, yellow, or green are best. Avoid dark or dull colors.

questions.question: When should you increase your following distance?

options.text: When the pavement is dry.
When riding conditions are normal.
When the roadway is wet.
When you can see through the vehicle in front of you.

questions.correctAnswerText: When the roadway is wet.
questions.explanation: Increase your following distance when your motorcycle will need more space to stop. You should also increase it in heavy traffic or when you cannot see around the vehicle in front of you.

questions.question: When does alcohol begin to impair your ability to ride?

options.text: Well below the legal limit.
Once you reach the legal limit.
Just above the legal limit.
Well above the legal limit.

questions.correctAnswerText: Well below the legal limit.
questions.explanation: Never ride after drinking any amount of alcohol. Impairment starts well below the legal limit.

questions.question: When do most motorcycle crashes happen?

options.text: At high speeds.
After riding for a long time.
Far from home.
On short trips.

questions.correctAnswerText: On short trips.
questions.explanation: Most motorcycle crashes happen on short trips of less than five miles at speeds under 30 miles per hour.

questions.question: How much stopping power does the front brake provide?

options.text: About 25 percent
About 50 percent
About 70 percent
100 percent

questions.correctAnswerText: About 70 percent
questions.explanation: The front brake is more powerful than the rear brake. It provides at least 70 percent of your motorcycle's total stopping power.

questions.question: Is it legal to ride between two vehicles moving in the same direction?

options.text: No, it is illegal.
Yes, if traffic is heavy.
Yes, during the day to prevent traffic jams.
Yes, if the rider is comfortable with it.

questions.correctAnswerText: No, it is illegal.
questions.explanation: In Oregon, motorcycles and mopeds cannot pass between two moving vehicles on a multilane highway or one-way street.

questions.question: What should your lane position do?

options.text: Keep you out of other drivers' blind spots.
Give you a good view of the shoulder.
Block your view of road hazards.
Encourage others to share your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep you out of other drivers' blind spots.
questions.explanation: Your lane position should help you see other drivers and help them see you. Do not stay in another driver's blind spot for long.

questions.question: If your motorcycle starts to wobble, what should you do?

options.text: Speed up to get out of the wobble.
Use the brakes slowly.
Hold the handlebars firmly and slowly close the throttle.
Shift to a lower gear.

questions.correctAnswerText: Hold the handlebars firmly and slowly close the throttle.
questions.explanation: Speeding up will make the wobble worse and is dangerous. Instead, hold the handlebars firmly without fighting the wobble. Slowly close the throttle to slow down. Move your weight forward and down. Pull off the road as soon as you safely can.

questions.question: What does making eye contact with other drivers mean?

options.text: It is the best way to know they see you.
It is not worth the effort.
It does not guarantee they will yield to you when they should.
It guarantees they will yield to you.

questions.correctAnswerText: It does not guarantee they will yield to you when they should.
questions.explanation: Never assume eye contact means a driver will yield to you. Drivers often look directly at motorcyclists but fail to see them.

questions.question: When riding at night, what should you do?

options.text: Change your lane position as needed for the conditions.
Ride faster than usual to reach your destination quickly.
Always use your low beam headlight for better visibility.
Follow closer to the vehicle ahead so you stay close.

questions.correctAnswerText: Change your lane position as needed for the conditions.
questions.explanation: Always adjust your lane position based on what you see, especially at night. Use safe riding practices when conditions are less than ideal.

questions.question: When you turn, what happens to traction for stopping?

options.text: There is less traction available for stopping.
There is more traction available for stopping.
Stopping is the same as on a straight road.
You should never try to stop while turning.

questions.correctAnswerText: There is less traction available for stopping.
questions.explanation: You can brake while turning, but it requires great care. When your motorcycle leans to turn, some traction is used for turning. This means less traction is available for braking.

questions.question: If you must swerve to avoid a hazard, what should you do?

options.text: Shift your weight quickly.
Turn your handlebars quickly.
Press the handlebar grip in the direction you want to turn.
Press the handlebar grip opposite to the direction you want to turn.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handlebar grip in the direction you want to turn.
questions.explanation: Apply light pressure to the handlebar grip in the direction of your swerve. To swerve left, press the left grip, then the right to straighten. To swerve right, press the right grip, then the left.

questions.question: Where should you place a load on your motorcycle?

options.text: As low as possible.
As high as possible.
Behind the rear axle.
On one side of the motorcycle.

questions.correctAnswerText: As low as possible.
questions.explanation: Keep loads low and secure them or place them in saddlebags. Do not pile loads high or against the sissy bar, as this raises your motorcycle's center of gravity and affects balance. Distribute weight equally on both sides.

questions.question: What is usually the best way to handle a tailgater?

options.text: Move onto the shoulder to get out of their way.
Speed up to create distance between you and them.
Ignore them.
Change lanes and let them pass.

questions.correctAnswerText: Change lanes and let them pass.
questions.explanation: The best way to handle a tailgater is to get them in front of you. If it is safe, change lanes and let them pass. Speeding up may only increase danger by encouraging them to follow faster.

questions.question: When crossing railroad tracks that run parallel to the road, how should you cross?

options.text: Cross at a 90-degree angle.
Avoid crossing the tracks.
Cross at a 45-degree angle or greater.
Cross slowly and inch your way across.

questions.correctAnswerText: Cross at a 45-degree angle or greater.
questions.explanation: Position yourself to cross railroad tracks, trolley tracks, or pavement seams at a 45-degree angle or greater. Make a quick, sharp turn. If you edge across slowly, the tracks or seams can catch your tires and throw you off balance.

questions.question: On a motorcycle with a sidecar, where should your passenger ride?

options.text: On the motorcycle seat.
In the sidecar.
Either on the motorcycle or in the sidecar.
Neither on the motorcycle nor in the sidecar.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the sidecar.
questions.explanation: Your passenger should ride in the sidecar. They should keep their hands inside the sidecar at all times.

questions.question: The center of a lane often has an oily strip. Is this area safe for motorcyclists?

options.text: Never safe for motorcyclists.
Usually safe unless the road is wet.
Usually safe unless it is sunny.
Always safe no matter the weather.

questions.correctAnswerText: Usually safe unless the road is wet.
questions.explanation: Oil from cars collects in a strip down the center of traffic lanes. When the road is dry, this area provides enough traction for safe riding. When the road is wet, it becomes slippery. Since the strip is usually only two feet wide, you can often ride to one side and still stay in the center portion of the lane.
